text: Where has your beloved gone, most beautiful of women? Which way has your beloved turned, that we may seek him with you?
My beloved has gone down to his garden, to the beds of spices, to graze in the gardens and to gather lilies.
I am my beloved's and my beloved is mine; he grazes among the lilies.
You are as beautiful as Tirzah, my love, as lovely as Jerusalem, awesome as an army with banners.

versions.text: You are beautiful, my love, as Tirzah, lovely as Jerusalem, awesome as an army with banners.
versions.explanation: "beautiful, my love, as Tirzah" separates the comparison awkwardly for a reader; placing the comparative phrase together reads more smoothly aloud and matches the parallel structure of the Hebrew line.

text: Turn your eyes away from me, for they overwhelm me. Your hair is like a flock of goats streaming down from Gilead.
Your teeth are like a flock of ewes coming up from the washing, each one bearing twins, and not one among them bereaved.
Your cheek behind your veil is like a slice of pomegranate.
There are sixty queens and eighty concubines, and maidens beyond number—

but she is the only one, my dove, my perfect one, the only child of her mother, the favorite of the one who bore her. The daughters saw her and called her blessed; the queens and concubines praised her.
Who is this that shines forth like the dawn, beautiful as the moon, bright as the sun, awesome as an army with banners?

versions.text: Who is this that looks down like the dawn, beautiful as the moon, bright as the sun, awesome as an army with banners?
versions.explanation: The verb here pictures appearing or breaking into view; "looks down" suggests she is gazing downward at something, which misdirects the image of the dawn rising into sight.

text: I went down to the nut orchard to see the new growth of the valley, to see whether the vine had budded, whether the pomegranates were in bloom.

versions.text: I went down to the nut orchard to see the blossoms of the valley, to see whether the vine had budded, whether the pomegranates were in bloom.
versions.explanation: The Hebrew term refers to fresh green shoots rather than blossoms; using "blossoms" here also duplicates the imagery of "in bloom" later in the same verse.

text: Before I knew it, my desire had set me among the chariots of my princely people.
